title: CSS: style your web pages
summary: Turn plain HTML into pages that look good and read well: colours, fonts, spacing, Flexbox layouts and responsive designs that work on a small phone first. Every lesson has a short example you can change and run.
outcomes: Write CSS rules with selectors, properties and values, and predict which rule wins
Style text with readable colours, fonts and sizes
Control spacing with the box model and arrange items with Flexbox
Make a page responsive with the viewport tag and mobile-first media queries
Add hover effects, transitions and shadows while keeping good contrast, and organise your styles so they are easy to update

chapters.title: How CSS works
chapters.goal: Write CSS rules, add CSS to a page in three ways and predict which rule wins when rules clash.

sections.heading: Your first CSS rule
sections.body:
CSS stands for Cascading Style Sheets. It controls how HTML looks: colours, fonts, spacing and layout. A CSS **rule** has two parts:

- a **selector**, which picks the elements to style, such as `h1`
- a block of **declarations** inside curly brackets. Each declaration is a **property** and a **value**, joined by a colon and ended with a semicolon, such as `color: darkgreen;`

CSS uses American spelling, so the property is `color`, never colour. The first line inside the style block is a **comment**, a note for people that the browser ignores. Run the example, then change the colour names and the sizes and watch what happens.

sections.heading: Selectors: choosing what to style
sections.body:
The selector decides which elements a rule affects: - `p` (a type selector) picks every `

`. - `.notice` (a class selector) picks every element with `class="notice"`. Many elements can share a class, and one element can have several classes. - `#top` (an id selector) picks the one element with `id="top"`. An id must be unique on the page. - `h1, h2` (a selector list) picks both kinds of heading. - `nav a` (a descendant selector) picks only the links that are inside a `

`. The dot and the hash appear only in the CSS, never in the HTML attribute. In the example, notice that the last link is not purple, because it is not inside the nav.

sections.heading: The cascade: which rule wins?
sections.body:
Sometimes two rules give the same element different values. The browser settles the clash with the **cascade**:

1. **Specificity**: a more precise selector beats a less precise one. An id beats a class, and a class beats a type selector such as `p`.
2. **Order**: if two selectors are equally specific, the rule that comes later wins.
3. An inline `style` attribute beats the rules in style sheets.

Some properties are also **inherited**: if you set `color` or `font-family` on `body`, the elements inside take it too. Properties such as `border` and `padding` are not inherited. Predict the colour of each line below before you run the example.

points: A rule is a selector followed by declarations in curly brackets: p { color: navy; }
Use an external stylesheet for real sites; one file can style every page
.name selects a class, #name selects an id, and p selects every paragraph
When rules clash, the more specific selector wins; if they are equally specific, the later rule wins
Some properties, such as color and font-family, are inherited by the elements inside
mistakes: Leaving out the semicolon between declarations — the browser cannot read that declaration or the one after it.
Writing the dot in the HTML, as in class=".notice" — the dot belongs only in the CSS selector.
Spelling a property the British way, such as colour — CSS ignores it; write color.
Using the same id on several elements — ids must be unique, so use a class for repeated styles.

quiz.q: A style block contains p { color: blue; } and then p { color: green; }. What colour is a plain paragraph?
opts: A mix of blue and green
Black, because the rules cancel out

quiz.q:
The CSS has p { color: blue; } and .notice { color: red; }. What colour is

?

quiz.q: What is wrong with h1 { color: darkgreen font-size: 30px; }?

font-size cannot be used on headings
Colour names must be written in capital letters
A rule can only contain one property

quiz.q: Which HTML element is selected by .price?

quiz.q: Why is an external stylesheet usually best for a site with five pages?

Browsers only understand CSS that is in a separate file
It lets the HTML files load without any CSS
Inline styles do not work on phones
quiz.why: All the pages link to the same file, so you edit one place and the browser can reuse its saved copy.

chapters.title: Colours, fonts and text
chapters.goal: Choose colours and fonts that are readable, load quickly and suit your page.

sections.heading: Ways to write colours
sections.body:
CSS understands colours written in several ways:

- **Names** such as `green`, `navy` or `tomato`. They are easy to read, but there is only a fixed list of them.
- **Hex codes** such as `#008751`. The six digits are three pairs for red, green and blue, from `00` (none) to `ff` (full). `#000000` is black and `#ffffff` is white.
- **rgb()** such as `rgb(0 135 81)`, which gives the same three amounts as numbers from 0 to 255. Adding a slash and a fourth value, as in `rgb(0 135 81 / 20%)`, makes the colour see-through.

`color` sets the text colour and `background-color` sets the colour behind it. Change them as a pair so the text stays readable.

code.source:
Independence Day Quiz

New Entries close on Friday.

This box uses a see-through green.

sections.heading: Fonts and sizes
sections.body:
`font-family` takes a list of fonts. The browser uses the first one the device has, so always end the list with a **generic family** such as `sans-serif`, `serif` or `monospace`. Fonts already on the device cost no data. Web fonts downloaded from the internet can look special, but each one adds to the page's download size, so use them sparingly.

For sizes, `px` (pixels) is fixed, while `rem` is relative to the root text size, which is usually 16px, so `1.5rem` is usually 24px. `rem` sizes grow when someone chooses a bigger text size in their browser settings, which helps people with low vision. `line-height: 1.5` puts comfortable space between lines, and `font-weight: 700` (or `bold`) makes text heavier.

code.source:
Coding Club

We meet in the computer room. Bring your notebook.

Today we learn the h1 element.

Snacks cost ₦300 and are optional.

sections.heading: Styling text for reading
sections.body:
A few more text properties make a big difference:

- `text-align` lines text up `left`, `right` or `center` (American spelling again). Keep long paragraphs left-aligned, because centred paragraphs are hard to read.
- `text-transform: uppercase` shows letters as capitals without changing your HTML.
- `letter-spacing` adds space between letters, which suits short headings.
- `text-decoration` adds or removes lines such as underlines. Keep the underline on links inside paragraphs so people can tell they are links.
- `max-width: 60ch` keeps lines to roughly 60 characters. Very long lines are tiring to read on big screens.

The `ch` unit is the width of the 0 character in the current font.

code.source:
Mama Ngozi's Provisions

We sell bread, tea, sugar and soft drinks near the school gate. See our full price list.

Bread: ₦1,200

A hex colour such as #008751 gives red, green and blue in pairs of digits
List several fonts and end with a generic family such as sans-serif
rem sizes follow the reader's chosen text size; 1rem is usually 16px
A line-height of about 1.5 makes paragraphs easier to read on a phone
mistakes: Leaving out the unit, as in font-size: 16 — the browser ignores the declaration; write 16px or 1rem.
Pale grey text on a white background — check the contrast so everyone can read it.
Loading several web fonts — each one costs data; system fonts are free and appear instantly.
Removing the underline from links inside paragraphs — readers can no longer tell which words are links.

quiz.why: The pairs are red 00, green aa and blue 00, so only green has any amount.

quiz.q: A page uses font-family: Ubuntu, Arial, sans-serif; and the phone has neither Ubuntu nor Arial. What happens?
opts: The browser uses the phone's default sans-serif font
quiz.why: The browser works along the list and falls back to the generic family at the end.

quiz.q: The root text size is 16px. How big is text set to 1.5rem?
quiz.why: 1.5rem means 1.5 times the root size: 1.5 × 16 = 24px.

quiz.q: Why does h1 { font-size: 32; } have no effect?
opts: The value has no unit such as px or rem, so the browser ignores it
32 is too big for a heading
Rules for h1 must use capital letters
quiz.why: Most lengths need a unit. Only 0 can be written without one.

quiz.q: Which pair of declarations gives a light green box with dark, readable text?
quiz.why: A pale background with near-black text has strong contrast. The others are pale on pale, dark on dark, or use properties that do not exist.

chapters.title: The box model
chapters.goal: Control spacing and size using content, padding, border, margin and box-sizing.

sections.heading: Every element is a box
sections.body:
The browser draws every element as a rectangular box with four layers, from the inside out:

1. **Content**: the text or image itself.
2. **Padding**: space inside the box, between the content and the border. The background colour fills it.
3. **Border**: a line around the padding.
4. **Margin**: space outside the border that pushes other boxes away. It is always see-through.

Think of a framed picture on a wall: the picture is the content, the card mount around it is the padding, the frame is the border and the gap to the next picture is the margin. When the bottom margin of one box meets the top margin of the box below, the browser uses only the larger of the two, so the gap between these cards is 30px, not 60px. Change each number in the example and watch which space grows.

code.source:
Cultural Day

Wear your traditional outfit on Friday.

The padding is inside the border; the margin is outside it.

sections.heading: Width, height and box-sizing
sections.body:
You can set `width` and `height`, but by default `width` measures only the **content**. Padding and border are added on top, so a box with `width: 200px`, `padding: 20px` and a `5px` border is really 250px wide. That surprises almost everyone at first.

Add `box-sizing: border-box` and the width includes the padding and border, so the box is exactly 200px wide. Many developers put this rule at the top of their stylesheet so it applies to every element: `* { box-sizing: border-box; }`

On phones, avoid fixed widths that may be wider than the screen. Use `max-width` instead: `max-width: 400px` means at most 400px, but narrower if the screen is smaller.

code.source:
content-box: 250px wide in total
border-box: exactly 200px wide

sections.heading: Shorthand, centring and rounded corners
sections.body:
`margin` and `padding` accept one to four values:

- `margin: 10px;` puts 10px on all four sides.
- `margin: 10px 20px;` puts 10px on the top and bottom and 20px on the left and right.
- `margin: 5px 10px 15px 20px;` goes clockwise from the top: top, right, bottom, left.

`margin: 20px auto;` centres a block that has a `width` or `max-width`, because the browser shares the leftover space equally between the left and right. The `border` shorthand takes a width, a style and a colour, such as `border: 2px solid green;`. Without a style such as `solid`, `dashed` or `dotted`, no border appears. `border-radius` rounds the corners.

code.source:
Excursion ticket

Trip to the National Museum, Lagos

Price: ₦2,500

points: From the inside out, a box has content, padding, border and margin
Padding is space inside the border; margin is space outside it
With box-sizing: border-box, width includes the padding and the border
margin: 0 auto centres a block that has a width or max-width
Four-value shorthand goes clockwise: top, right, bottom, left
mistakes: Setting width: 100% and adding padding, which creates a sideways scroll — use box-sizing: border-box.
Using padding when you want space between two cards — space between boxes is margin.
Giving boxes fixed widths such as width: 800px — on a phone, use max-width so the box can shrink.
Writing border: 2px green without a style — add solid, dashed or dotted, or no border appears.
chapters.task: Make a ticket or ID-card style box for a school event: give it padding, a border and rounded corners, centre it with margin and auto, and limit its width with max-width. Then remove box-sizing or add it, and explain to yourself why the size changes.

quiz.q: A box has width: 200px; padding: 10px; and border: 5px solid; with the default box-sizing. How wide is it on screen, not counting margin?
quiz.why: The default content-box adds padding on both sides (20px) and border on both sides (10px): 200 + 20 + 10 = 230px.

quiz.q: The same box is given box-sizing: border-box. How wide is it now?
quiz.why: With border-box, the 200px width already includes the padding and border, so the content area shrinks instead.

quiz.q: In margin: 10px 20px 30px 40px; what is the left margin?
quiz.why: Four values go clockwise from the top: top 10px, right 20px, bottom 30px, left 40px.

quiz.q: Why does border: 3px green; show no border at all?
opts: It is missing a border style such as solid
quiz.why: The shorthand sets the style to none when you leave it out, and a border with no style is not drawn.

quiz.q: Two cards are touching each other. Which change adds space between them without changing the space inside each card?
quiz.why: Margin is the space outside the border, so it pushes the cards apart. Padding would make each card bigger inside.

chapters.title: Display and Flexbox layout
chapters.goal: Understand block and inline boxes and use Flexbox to arrange items in rows that wrap on small screens.

sections.heading: Block, inline and inline-block
sections.body:
Every element has a `display` type: - **Block** elements, such as `

`, `

`, `
` and `
`, start on a new line and stretch across the full width available. - **Inline** elements, such as ``, `` and ``, sit inside a line of text and are only as wide as their content. `width` and `height` have no effect on them. - `display: inline-block` keeps an element in the line but lets you set its width, height and padding, which is handy for small badges. You can change any element's type, for example by making links `display: block`. `display: none` removes an element from the page completely, and screen readers skip it too.

A span ignores width but a badge obeys it.

You cannot see me.

sections.heading: Flexbox: items in a row
sections.body:
**Flexbox** is a layout tool for arranging items in a row or a column. You switch it on by giving the **parent** `display: flex`. Its direct children then become **flex items** and line up in a row.

Three properties on the parent do most of the work:

- `gap` sets the space between items.
- `justify-content` spreads items along the row, with values such as `flex-start`, `center`, `space-between` and `flex-end`.
- `align-items` lines items up across the row; `center` is useful for lining up items of different heights.

A navigation bar is a perfect first job for Flexbox. Try changing `space-between` to `center` or `flex-end`.

code.source: JETS Club Projects Join

sections.heading: Wrapping cards for small screens
sections.body:
On a phone there is not enough room for many items in one row. `flex-wrap: wrap` lets items move onto a new line when they run out of space.

The `flex` property on each item says how it should size itself. `flex: 1 1 150px` means: start at about 150px wide, **grow** to share any spare space and **shrink** if needed. With this, the cards sit side by side on a wide screen and stack on a narrow one, without any extra code.

`flex-direction: column` stacks the items from top to bottom instead, while keeping `gap` and the alignment controls. Change `150px` to `300px` and run the example again to watch the cards rearrange.

code.source:
Robotics
Solar cooker
Water filter
Weather station

points: Block elements stack and fill the width; inline elements flow inside a line of text
display: flex goes on the parent, and its direct children become flex items
justify-content spaces items along the row; align-items lines them up across it
flex-wrap: wrap lets items move onto a new line when space runs out
gap sets the space between flex items without extra margins
mistakes: Putting display: flex on the items instead of their parent — the container is the one that needs it.
Expecting width to work on an inline span — make it inline-block or block first.
Forgetting flex-wrap, so cards squash into a thin row on phones — add flex-wrap: wrap.
Using display: none on content everyone needs — it hides it from screen readers as well.

You want the links in

in a row with space between them. Where should display: flex go?

quiz.q: In a flex row, which declaration on the parent pushes all the items to the right-hand end?
quiz.why: justify-content works along the row. align-items works across it, so flex-end there moves items to the bottom.

quiz.q: Four cards with flex: 1 1 200px sit in a 360px-wide container with flex-wrap: wrap and no gap. How do they appear?

Four cards squeezed into one row
Two cards per row, each 200px wide

quiz.q: What does display: none do to an element?
opts: Removes it from the page and the layout, and screen readers skip it too
Makes it see-through but keeps its space
Turns it into an inline element
quiz.why: With display: none, the element takes up no space and is not shown or read out at all.

quiz.q: The rule span { width: 120px; } has no visible effect on a <span>. Why?

Spans can only be styled with classes

chapters.title: Responsive design
chapters.goal: Make a page that fits phones first and adapts to bigger screens with media queries.

sections.heading: The viewport meta tag
sections.body:
Many phone browsers were designed when most pages were built for computers. Without instructions, they may lay your page out on a wide imaginary screen (980px wide, for example) and then shrink it, leaving tiny text that people must pinch to read.

This line in the `<head>` tells the browser to use the device's real width at normal zoom:

`<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">`

Put it in every page you make. Never add `user-scalable=no` or `maximum-scale=1`: blocking zoom stops people with low vision from enlarging your text. The preview box behaves like its own small screen whether or not the tag is there, so check the tag on a real phone.

code.source:
Kano Science Fair

This banner is never wider than 600px, but it shrinks to fit a small phone.

sections.heading: Media queries
sections.body:
A **media query** wraps rules that apply only when a condition is true. The most useful condition is the width of the viewport:

`@media (min-width: 500px) { ... }`

The rules inside the curly brackets apply only when the viewport is at least 500px wide. The width at which your layout changes is called a **breakpoint**. Real sites often use breakpoints such as 600px or 768px; these examples use 500px so you can see a change in the small preview box.

The preview measures its own width, not your whole screen. Change `500px` to `300px` or `900px`, run the example again and watch the links switch between a stack and a row.

code.source:
Home Events Gallery Join

On a narrow screen the links stack. On a wider one they sit in a row.

sections.heading: Mobile-first design
sections.body:
**Mobile-first** means you write the basic styles for small screens first, with everything in one column, and then add `min-width` media queries to rearrange things on bigger screens. Phones get the simplest layout, and you add complexity only where there is room for it.

A few habits keep pages flexible:

- Use `max-width` and percentages instead of fixed widths.
- Add `img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; }` so pictures never spill off the screen.
- Make buttons and links big enough to tap with a thumb.
- Put each media query after the rules it changes, because a later rule with the same specificity wins.

On a computer, Chrome, Edge and Firefox can preview phone sizes: press F12 to open the developer tools, then Ctrl + Shift + M for the device or responsive mode.

code.source:
Club news

Our solar cooker project came second at the state science fair.

Next meeting

Friday, 2 p.m.

points: Put <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"> in the head of every page
A media query applies its rules only when its condition, such as a minimum width, is true
Mobile-first means base styles for phones, then min-width queries for larger screens
img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; } stops pictures spilling off small screens
Never block zooming; people with low vision need it

Forgetting the curly brackets that wrap the rules inside @media — every rule inside must sit between them.

Designing only on a laptop and checking the phone last — start with the phone layout.

Yes, because media queries apply everywhere
Yes, but only after the page is refreshed
No, because phones cannot use Flexbox
quiz.why: min-width: 600px is false at 400px, so the browser skips the rules inside the query.

quiz.q: Which approach is mobile-first?
opts: One-column base styles, then @media (min-width: 700px) adds columns
Three-column base styles, then @media (max-width: 700px) removes columns
Only desktop styles, with no media queries
Separate pages for phones and computers
quiz.why: Mobile-first starts with the small-screen layout and uses min-width queries to add to it.

quiz.q: A photo 1200px wide spills off a phone screen. Which CSS fixes it?
quiz.why: max-width: 100% stops the image being wider than its container, and height: auto keeps its shape.

quiz.q: Without a viewport meta tag, what may a phone browser do with your page?
opts: Lay it out on a wide imaginary screen and shrink it, making the text tiny
Turn it into a single column automatically
quiz.why: Many phone browsers assume an old desktop-width page and zoom out to fit it, unless the viewport tag says otherwise.

quiz.q: The CSS has .card { width: 100%; }, then @media (min-width: 600px) { .card { width: 50%; } }, then .card { width: 100%; } at the very end. Why are cards never half width?
opts: The last rule has the same specificity and comes later, so it always wins
A media query must be the first rule in the file
quiz.why: Media queries do not add specificity. When the query matches, its rule still loses to an equally specific rule that comes after it.

chapters.title: Polish: hover, transitions, shadows and contrast
chapters.goal: Add small, accessible finishing touches that make a page feel friendly and easy to read.

sections.heading: States: :hover, :focus-visible and :active
sections.body:
A **pseudo-class** styles an element when it is in a certain state. You write it after the selector with a colon:

- `:hover` applies while a mouse pointer is over the element.
- `:focus-visible` applies when someone reaches the element with the keyboard, so they can see where they are.
- `:active` applies while the element is being pressed.

Touch screens have no real hover, so never hide important information that only appears on hover. Always keep a visible focus style: if you remove the browser's outline, replace it with something just as clear.

code.source: Hover over the button, press it, or tap the preview and press Tab to see each state.

sections.heading: Smooth changes with transition
sections.body:
Without help, a hover colour changes instantly. `transition` makes the change happen smoothly over a short time:

`transition: background-color 0.2s ease;`

This names the property to animate, how long the change takes and its speed curve. Short times of about 0.15 to 0.3 seconds feel quick and responsive; long ones feel slow. `transform` can move or resize an element without disturbing the layout around it; for example, `transform: translateY(-4px)` lifts a card slightly.

Some people feel dizzy or sick when things move on screen. The media query `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` lets you switch movement off for anyone who has asked their device for less motion.

code.source:
Art Club exhibition

Move a mouse pointer over this card to lift it.

sections.heading: Shadows and rounded corners
sections.body:
`box-shadow` draws a shadow behind a box. Its values are, in order: how far the shadow moves sideways, how far it moves down, how blurred it is, and its colour. For example, `box-shadow: 0 2px 8px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.15);` makes a soft shadow just below the box. A small, pale shadow looks modern; a big black one looks heavy.

`border-radius` rounds corners: `8px` gives gentle curves, and `50%` on a square makes a circle. `text-shadow` works in a similar way for text, but use it rarely, because it can make text blurry and harder to read.

code.source:
Club captain

Leads our Friday meetings.

sections.heading: Colour contrast
sections.body:
**Contrast** is the difference in brightness between text and its background. Low contrast, such as light grey on white, is hard to read, especially on a phone in bright sunshine or for people with low vision.

The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) set minimum contrast ratios. For level AA:

- normal text needs at least **4.5:1**
- large text (about 24px, or about 19px if bold) needs at least **3:1**

You do not need to work this out yourself: the free WebAIM Contrast Checker gives the ratio for any two colours. Also, never use colour alone to give a message. Add words or a symbol, such as Sold out, rather than only turning a price red.

points: :hover styles a pointer hovering, :focus-visible shows keyboard focus and :active shows a press
transition makes changes smooth; keep it short, around 0.2 seconds
box-shadow takes a sideways offset, a downward offset, a blur and a colour
Under WCAG AA, normal text needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 with its background
Respect prefers-reduced-motion for people who are troubled by movement
mistakes: Removing the focus outline with outline: none and giving nothing in its place — keyboard users get lost.
Menus or information that appear only on hover — phones and other touch screens cannot hover.

chapters.task: Style a button for your club page with :hover, :focus-visible and :active states and a 0.2-second transition. Then check your text and button colours in the WebAIM Contrast Checker and change any pair that scores below 4.5:1.

quiz.q: The CSS has button { transition: background-color 0.2s; } and button:hover { background-color: navy; }. What happens when a mouse pointer moves over the button?
opts: The background fades to navy over 0.2 seconds
The button turns navy instantly and stays navy for ever
The button waits 0.2 seconds and then disappears
Nothing, because transition only works on text
quiz.why: The hover rule changes the colour, and the transition spreads that change over 0.2 seconds. It fades back when the pointer leaves.

quiz.q: In box-shadow: 0 4px 10px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.2); what does 4px do?
opts: Moves the shadow 4px to the right
quiz.why: The first value is the sideways offset (0), the second is the downward offset (4px) and the third is the blur (10px).

quiz.q: Grey text (#999999) on white has a contrast ratio of about 2.8:1. Does it meet WCAG AA for a normal paragraph?
opts: No, normal text needs at least 4.5:1
Yes, grey always passes on white
No, because grey text is never allowed
quiz.why: AA requires 4.5:1 for normal-sized text, so 2.8:1 is too low. A darker grey would pass.

quiz.q: A menu only opens when the pointer hovers over the word Clubs. What problem will phone users have?
opts: Touch screens cannot hover, so the menu may be hard or impossible to open
The menu opens on every page automatically
Phones cannot display menus at all
quiz.why: There is no pointer resting over the screen on a touch device, so make menus open with a tap or click as well.

quiz.q: A designer adds button:focus { outline: none; } and nothing else. Who is most affected?
opts: People using a keyboard, who can no longer see which button is selected
People using a mouse, who cannot click the button
Search engines, which cannot find the button
Nobody, because outlines are only decoration
quiz.why: The focus outline shows keyboard users where they are. Removing it without a replacement leaves them guessing.

chapters.title: Organising your styles
chapters.goal: Write reusable, well-named and well-commented CSS that is easy to update.

sections.heading: Reusable classes
sections.body:
As a site grows, writing a separate rule for every element becomes messy. Instead, create **classes** that describe a job and reuse them wherever that job appears: `.card` for boxes of content, `.button` for buttons and button-like links, `.notice` for important messages.

An element can have several classes, separated by spaces: `class="button button-small"`. This lets you keep one basic class and add small extras, often called **modifiers**.

Name classes by their **purpose**, not their appearance. If you call a class `.red-text` and later decide the colour should be blue, the name becomes misleading. `.warning` stays true whatever colour you choose.

code.source: Join the club Read the rules Photos

sections.heading: Custom properties (CSS variables)
sections.body:
When the same colour or size appears in many rules, store it once in a **custom property**. Its name starts with two hyphens, and you usually set it on `:root`, which stands for the whole page:

`:root { --brand: #008751; }`

Read it anywhere with `var()`, as in `color: var(--brand);`. Change the value in one place and every rule that uses it updates, so you can try a new colour scheme for your club page in seconds.

Custom property names are case-sensitive: `--brand` and `--Brand` are different. If you misspell a name inside `var()`, the browser finds no value and the style does not work as planned.

sections.heading: Comments and a clear order
sections.body:
Comments, like the numbered labels in the example, explain **why** something is there or label the parts of a long file. Every CSS comment starts with a slash and a star and ends with a star and a slash. CSS has no `//` comments; writing one breaks the rule that follows it.

Keeping the same order in every stylesheet helps you find things quickly:

1. Custom properties on `:root`
2. Base styles for elements such as `body`, `h1` and `a`
3. Layout, such as the header, main area and footer
4. Reusable components such as `.card` and `.button`
5. Media queries for bigger screens

Delete rules you no longer use, and keep your styles in the stylesheet rather than scattered in `style` attributes. Tidy code is easier to fix, and easier for someone else to help you with.

quiz.q: The CSS has :root { --brand: green; } and h1 { color: var(--brand); }. You change --brand to purple. What happens?
opts: Every rule that uses var(--brand) turns purple
Only the first h1 turns purple
Nothing changes until you also edit the h1 rule
The page shows an error, because variables cannot change
quiz.why: var(--brand) reads the current value, so changing it in one place updates every rule that uses it.

quiz.q: Why does this CSS fail to style the header? // Header styles header { background-color: navy; }

The header element cannot have a background colour
navy is not a valid colour name
Comments must come after the rule, not before it

quiz.q: In a mobile-first stylesheet, where should a media query for wide screens usually go?
opts: After the base styles it changes
Inside the HTML instead of the stylesheet
In a comment, so phones skip it
quiz.why: Placed later, the query's rules override the base styles when the screen is wide enough.

project.title: Style your club page for phones and computers
project.brief: Give the club page you built in the HTML course a clear, attractive design that works on a small phone first and adapts to bigger screens. Keep all your styles in one external stylesheet, so that the JavaScript course can add an interactive feature to the same page.
steps: Create styles.css in your club-site folder and link it in the head of index.html with <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">.
At the top of styles.css, add * { box-sizing: border-box; } and custom properties on :root for two or three club colours.
Style the base: a system font stack ending in sans-serif, line-height around 1.5, and a main area with max-width and margin: 0 auto.
Turn the nav into a Flexbox row with gap, and make your activity sections into cards that wrap with flex-wrap.
Style the table and the form: borders and padding for the table, full-width inputs on phones, and a button with :hover and :focus-visible states.
Add a min-width media query that gives a wider layout on bigger screens.
Check text contrast with the WebAIM Contrast Checker and test the page at phone width and at computer width.
checklist: There is no sideways scrolling on a 360px-wide phone screen
Text and buttons have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1
Keyboard focus is clearly visible on links and buttons
All styles live in styles.css, grouped into commented sections
Images never spill out of their container
